content.thinking: This intervention frames climate scientists in a warm, community-member light, so I expect it to mainly lift benevolence and integrity trust, with a moderate 3-4 point bump on the primary trust measure and smaller anchored effects on post-trust and distrust. I'm estimating more modest shifts across funding perception, institutional trust, belief, concern, and policy attitudes, with behavioral outcomes like donations and newsletter signups barely moving.

parsed_output.reasoning_summary: The text is a warmth/benevolence-focused narrative that humanizes climate scientists as neighbors, parents, and local helpers, with concrete cooperative examples (Hurricane Harvey flood maps, wildfire spread models with fire crews). Its mechanism is boosting perceived benevolence and integrity (shared values, 'people like us') rather than correcting factual beliefs or addressing funding/bias concerns, so the largest movement should be on the multidimensional trust measure taken immediately after reading, with smaller effects on the single-item trust question that is anchored to a pre-treatment answer. Distrust items are typically stickier and partly capture ideological priors, so I expect a smaller-magnitude negative effect. Downstream attitudes (belief, concern, policy support, behavior) are heavily determined by prior partisanship and are only indirectly touched by a one-shot trust message, and belief/policy items also have anchoring or ceiling issues, so I put these at roughly a quarter to a third of the primary trust effect; the collaboration-with-emergency-managers framing gives policy_role a somewhat larger bump. Incentivized behaviors (donation, newsletter) show near-zero effects in such megastudies, so I forecast small fractions of a dollar and ~1 percentage point.
